title: Complete Binary Tree Inserter
statement:
A binary tree is **complete** when every level above the deepest one has all of its nodes, and the nodes of the deepest level are packed together on the left. Build a class `CBTInserter` that keeps such a tree complete while new nodes are added:

- `CBTInserter(root)` receives the root `TreeNode` (with `val`, `left` and `right`) of a complete binary tree.
- `insert(val)` attaches a new node holding `val` at the only position that leaves the tree complete, and returns the `val` of the node it was attached under.
- `get_root()` returns the root of the tree, including every node inserted so far.
constraints: The initial tree has between 1 and 1000 nodes
root is a complete binary tree
At most 10^4 calls are made to insert and get_root
notes:
## Intuition

Walking the tree to find the free slot on every insert costs O(n) each time. In a complete tree, the nodes that can still take a child are exactly the ones read in level order from some point on, and new nodes join the end of that same order. So a queue of "nodes missing a child", built once with a breadth-first pass, always has the next parent at its front.

## Approach

1. In the constructor, set `head = 0` and do a breadth-first pass over the tree (`order`). Every node missing a left or right child is appended to `queue`, in level order.
2. On `insert(val)`, the parent is `queue[head]`. Create the new node.
3. If the parent has no left child, attach it there. Otherwise attach it on the right; the parent is now full, so advance `head`.
4. The new node has no children yet, so append it to `queue`. Return the parent's value.
5. `get_root()` returns the stored root.

## Example 1, step by step

The tree is `1` with left child `2`. The breadth-first pass puts `1` (missing a right child) and `2` (a leaf) in `queue`, so `queue = [1, 2]` and `head = 0`. `insert(3)`: the parent is `1`, whose left is taken, so `3` goes on the right, `head` becomes 1, and `queue = [1, 2, 3]`; return `1`. `insert(4)`: the parent is `2`, whose left is free, so `4` becomes its left child; return `2`. `get_root()` gives the tree `[1, 2, 3, 4]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) for the constructor; O(1) for `insert` and `get_root`.
- Space: O(n + k) for the queue, with `k` the number of inserts.

## Pitfalls

- Only advance `head` after filling the **right** child; a parent with a free right slot must stay at the front.
- Push every new node onto the queue, or later inserts will skip a level.
- Use `queue.shift()` sparingly: it is O(n) per call in JavaScript, which is why a `head` index is used instead.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `root` | the root of the tree, returned by `get_root` |
| `order`, `i` | the breadth-first list built in the constructor, and the position being read in it |
| `queue` | nodes that can still take a child, in level order |
| `head` | index of the next parent in `queue` |
| `parent`, `node` | where the new node goes, and the new node itself |
